#Text=in one of the districts into which the island is divided, and several
#Text= precipices among the mountains, evidently produced by sudden violence,
#Text= indicate the volcanic origin of this highly favoured country.
#Text=There is
#Text= plenty of good water to be had over all the island.
#Text=The weather from
#Text= March till August is usually mild and pleasant.
#Text=During the rough season,
#Text= which lasts from December till March, the wind often blows very hard
#Text= from the west, and is attended with rain.
#Text=--E.]
#Text=The produce of this island is bread-fruit, cocoa-nuts, bananas of
#Text= thirteen sorts, the best we had ever eaten; plantains; a fruit not
#Text= unlike an apple, which, when ripe, is very pleasant; sweet potatoes,
#Text= yams, cocoas, a kind of _Arum_ fruit known here by the name of
#Text= _Jambu_, and reckoned most delicious; sugar-cane, which the inhabitants
#Text= eat raw; a root of the salop kind, called by the inhabitants _Pea_; a
#Text= plant called _Ethee_, of which the root only is eaten; a fruit that
#Text= grows in a pod, like that of a large kidney-bean, which, when it is
#Text= roasted, eats very much like a chesnut, by the natives called _Ahee_; a
#Text= tree called _Wharra_, called in the East Indies _Pandanes_, which
#Text= produces fruit, something like the pine-apple; a shrub called _Nono_;
#Text= the _Morinda_, which also produces fruit; a species of fern, of which
#Text=variety of fish.
#Text=The smaller fish, when they catch any, are generally
#Text= eaten raw, as we eat oysters; and nothing that the sea produces comes
#Text= amiss to them: They are fond of lobsters, crabs, and other shell-fish,
#Text= which are found upon the coast; and they will eat not only sea-insects,
#Text= but what the seamen call _blubbers_, though some of them are so tough,
#Text= that they are obliged, to suffer them to become putrid before they can
#Text= be chewed.
#Text=Of the many vegetables that have been mentioned already as
#Text= serving them for food, the principal is the bread-fruit, to procure
#Text= which costs them no trouble or labour but climbing a tree: The tree
#Text= which produces it, does not indeed shoot up spontaneously; but if a man
#Text= plants ten of them in his lifetime, which he may do in about an hour, he
#Text= will as completely fulfil his duty to his own and future generations, as
#Text= the natives of our less temperate climate can do by ploughing in the
#Text= cold of winter, and reaping in the summer  '  s heat, as often as these
#Text= seasons return; even if, after he has procured bread for his present
#Text= household, he should convert a surplus into money, and lay it up for his
#Text= children.
#Text=It is true, indeed, that the bread-fruit is not always in season; but
#Text= cocoa-nuts, bananas, plantains, and a great variety of other fruits,
#Text=supply the deficiency.
#Text=It may well be supposed, that cookery is but little studied by these
#Text= people as an art; and, indeed, they have but two ways of applying fire
#Text= to dress their food, broiling and baking; the operation of broiling is
#Text= so simple that it requires no description, and their baking has been
#Text= described already, in the account of an entertainment prepared for us by
#Text= Tupia.
#Text=Hogs and large fish are extremely well dressed in the same
#Text= manner; and, in our opinion, were more juicy, and more equally done,
#Text= than by any art of cookery now practised in Europe.
#Text=Bread-fruit is also
#Text= cooked in an oven of the same kind, which renders it soft, and something
#Text= like a boiled potatoe; not quite so farinaceous as a good one, but more
#Text= so than those of the middling sort.
#Text=Of the-bread-fruit they also make three dishes, by putting either water
#Text= or the milk of the cocoa-nut to it, then beating it to a paste with a
#Text= stone pestle, and afterwards mixing it with ripe plantains, bananas, or
#Text= the sour paste which they call _mahie_.
#Text=The mahie, which has been mentioned as a succedaneum for ripe
#Text=bread-fruit, before the season for gathering a fresh crop comes on, is
#Text= thus made:
#Text=
#Text= The fruit is gathered just before it is perfectly ripe, and being laid
#Text= in heaps, is closely covered with leaves; in this state it undergoes a
#Text= fermentation, and becomes disagreeably sweet: The core is then taken out
#Text= entire, which is done by gently pulling the stalk, and the rest of the
#Text= fruit is thrown into a hole which is dug for that purpose, generally in
#Text= the houses, and neatly lined in the bottom and sides with grass; the
#Text= whole is then covered with leaves, and heavy stones laid upon them: In
#Text= this state it undergoes a second fermentation, and becomes sour, after
#Text= which it will suffer no change for many months: It is taken out of the
#Text= hole as it is wanted for use, and being made into balls, it is wrapped
#Text= up in leaves and baked; after it is dressed, it will keep five or
#Text= six-weeks.
#Text=It is eaten both cold and hot, and the natives seldom make a
#Text= meal without it, though to us the taste was as disagreeable as that of a
#Text= pickled olive generally is the first time it is eaten.
#Text=As the making of this mahie depends, like brewing, upon fermentation,
#Text= so, like brewing, it sometimes fails, without their being able to
#Text=ascertain the cause; it is very natural, therefore, that the making it
#Text= should be connected with superstitious notions and ceremonies: It
#Text= generally falls to the lot of the old women, who will suffer no creature
#Text= to touch any thing belonging to it, but those whom they employ as
#Text= assistants, nor even to go into that part of the house where the
#Text= operation is carrying on.
#Text=Mr Banks happened to spoil a large quantity of
#Text= it only by inadvertently touching a leaf which lay upon it.
#Text=The old
#Text= woman, who then presided over these mysteries, told him, that the
#Text= process would fail; and immediately uncovered the hole in a fit of
#Text= vexation and despair.
#Text=Mr Banks regretted the mischief he had done, but
#Text= was somewhat consoled by the opportunity which it gave him of examining
#Text= the preparation, which perhaps, but for such an accident, would never
#Text= have offered.[9]
#Text=
#Text= [Footnote 9: "This paste," we are told in the missionary account, "makes
#Text= a most nutritious and sweet pudding, and all the children of the family
#Text= and their relations feast on it eagerly.
#Text=But though they would not eat with us or with each other, they have
#Text= often asked us to eat with them, when we have visited those with whom we
#Text= were particularly acquainted at their houses; and we have often upon
#Text= such occasions eaten out of the same basket, and drunk out of the same
#Text= cup.
#Text= and each sex invites by turns their companions to partake with them of
#Text= the food they happen to have."
#Text=He tells us, however, that in their
#Text= domestic way of living, the sexes usually associate.
#Text=Of the female
#Text= Charaibes, Mr Edwards, quoting Labat, says, that they were not allowed
#Text= the privilege of eating in presence of their husbands.
#Text=And Rochon, in
#Text= his account of Madagascar, tells us something to the same purport of the
#Text= women of that island.
#Text=It would be easy to multiply instances of the
#Text= custom which Hawkesworth thinks to be peculiar to the Otaheitans.
#Text=--E.]
#Text=After meals, and in the heat of the day, the middle-aged people of the
#Text= better sort generally sleep; they are indeed extremely indolent, and
#Text= sleeping and eating is almost all that they do.
#Text=Those that are older are
#Text= less drowsy, and the boys and girls are kept awake by the natural
#Text= activity and sprightliness of their age.
#Text=Their amusements have occasionally been mentioned in my account of the
#Text= incidents that happened during our residence in this island,
#Text=after a short time applied to their ordinary occupations, as if no
#Text= stranger had been among them.
#Text=In the forenoon, several of their boats
#Text= went out a-fishing, and at dinner time every one repaired to his
#Text= respective dwelling; from which, after a certain time, he returned.
#Text=These fair appearances encouraged Mr Banks and Dr Solander to range the
#Text= bay with very little precaution, where they found many plants, and shot
#Text= some birds of exquisite beauty.
#Text=In their walk, they visited several
#Text= houses of the natives, and saw something of their manner of life; for
#Text= they showed, without any reserve, every thing which the gentlemen
#Text= desired to see.
#Text=They were sometimes found at their meals, which the
#Text= approach of the strangers never interrupted.
#Text=Their food at this season
#Text= consisted of fish, with which, instead of bread, they eat the root of a
#Text= kind of fern, very like that which grows upon our commons in England.
#Text=These roots they scorch over the fire, and then beat with a stick, till
#Text= the bark and dry outside fall off; what remains is a soft substance,
#Text= somewhat clammy and sweet, not unpleasing to the taste, but mixed with
#Text= three or four times its quantity of strings and fibres, which are very
#Text= disagreeable; these were swallowed by some, but spit out by the far
#Text= greater number, who had baskets under them to receive the rejected part
#Text= of what had been chewed, which had an appearance very like that of
#Text=tobacco in the same state.
#Text=In other seasons they have certainly plenty
#Text= of excellent vegetables; but no tame animals were seen among them except
#Text= dogs, which were very small and ugly.
#Text=Mr Banks saw some of their
#Text= plantations, where the ground was as well broken down and tilled as even
#Text= in the gardens of the most curious people among us: In these spots were
#Text= sweet potatoes, coccos or eddas, which are well known and much esteemed
#Text= both in the East and West Indies, and some gourds: The sweet potatoes
#Text= were planted in small hills, some ranged in rows, and others in
#Text= quincunx, all laid by a line with the greatest regularity: The coccos
#Text= were planted upon flat land, but none of them yet appeared above ground;
#Text= and the gourds were set in small hollows, or dishes, much as in England.
#Text=These plantations were of different extent, from one or two acres to
#Text= ten: Taken together, there appeared to be from 150 to 200 acres in
#Text= cultivation in the whole bay, though we never saw an hundred people.
#Text=Each district was fenced in, generally with reeds, which were placed so
#Text= close together that there was scarcely room for a mouse to creep
#Text= between.
#Text=The women were plain, and made themselves more so by painting their
#Text= faces with red ochre and oil, which being generally fresh and wet upon
#Text=This afternoon, we set up the armourer  '  s forge, to repair the braces of
#Text= the tiller which had been broken, and went on getting our wood and
#Text= water, without suffering the least molestation from the natives; who
#Text= came down with different sorts of fish, which we purchased with cloth,
#Text= beads, and glass bottles, as usual.
#Text=On the 25th, Mr Banks and Dr Solander went again on shore; and while
#Text= they were searching for plants, Tupia staid with the waterers: Among
#Text= other Indians who came down to them was a priest, with whom Tupia
#Text= entered into a very learned conversation.
#Text=In their notions of religion
#Text= they seemed to agree very well, which is not often the case between
#Text= learned divines on our side of the ocean: Tupia, however, seemed to have
#Text= the most knowledge, and he was listened to with great deference and
#Text= attention by the other.
#Text=In the course of this conversation, after the
#Text= important points of divinity had been settled, Tupia enquired if it was
#Text= their practice to eat men, to which they answered in the affirmative;
#Text= but said that they eat only their enemies who were slain in battle.[58]
#Text=
#Text= [Footnote 58: There is some reason, however, to believe that they make
#Text= battle in order that they may have enemies to eat.
#Text=It is something like
#Text=abounded in cockles and clams: In many places there were rock oysters,
#Text= and everywhere plenty of wild fowl, principally shags, ducks, curlieus,
#Text= and the sea-pie, that, has been described before.
#Text=We also saw fish in
#Text= the river, but of what kind we could not discover: The country on the
#Text= east side of this river is for the most part barren and destitute of
#Text= wood; but on the west it has a better aspect, and in some places is
#Text= adorned with trees, but has in no part the appearance of cultivation.
#Text=In
#Text= the entrance of the river, and for two or three miles up, there is good
#Text= anchoring in four and five fathom water, and places very convenient for
#Text= laying a vessel on shore, where the tide rises and falls seven feet at
#Text= the full and change of the moon.
#Text=We could not determine whether any
#Text= considerable stream of fresh water came into this river out of the
#Text= country; but we saw a number of small rivulets issue from the adjacent
#Text= hills.
#Text=Near the mouth of this river, on the east side, we found a little
#Text= Indian village, consisting of small temporary sheds, where we landed,
#Text= and were received by the people with the utmost kindness and
#Text= hospitality: They treated us with a flat shell-fish of a most delicious
#Text= taste, somewhat like a cockle, which we eat hot from the coals.
#Text=Near
#Text= this place is a high point or peninsula, projecting into the river, and
#Text= upon it are the remains of a fort, which they call _eppah_, or _heppah_.
#Text=low; but in the middle of the island there are hills of a considerable
#Text= height.
#Text=We were upon the coast at the latter end of the dry season, when
#Text= there had been no rain for seven months; and we were told that when the
#Text= dry season continues so long, there is no running stream of fresh water
#Text= upon the whole island, but only small springs, which are at a
#Text= considerable distance from the sea-side; yet nothing can be imagined so
#Text= beautiful as the prospect of the country from the ship.
#Text=The level ground
#Text= next to the sea-side was covered with cocoa-nut trees, and a kind of
#Text= palm called _arecas_; and beyond them the hills, which rose in a gentle
#Text= and regular ascent, were richly clothed, quite to the summit, with
#Text= plantations of the fan-palm, forming an almost impenetrable grove.
#Text=How
#Text= much even this prospect must be improved, when every foot of ground
#Text= between the trees is covered with verdure, by maize, and millet, and
#Text= indigo, can scarcely be conceived but by a powerful imagination, not
#Text= unacquainted with the stateliness and beauty of the trees that adorn
#Text= this part of the earth.
#Text=The dry season commences in March or April, and
#Text= ends in October or November.

#Text= colour, and in the inside are a few seeds disposed in the form of a
#Text= star: Its flavour is a light, clean, pleasant acid, but it cannot be
#Text= eaten raw; it is said to be excellent as a pickle; and stewed, it made a
#Text= most agreeable sour sauce to our boiled dishes.
#Text=The tame animals are buffaloes, sheep, goats, hogs, fowls, pigeons,
#Text= horses, asses, dogs, and cats; and of all these there is great plenty.
#Text=The buffaloes differ very considerably from the horned cattle of Europe
#Text= in several particulars; their ears are much larger, their skins are
#Text= almost without hair, their horns are curved towards each other, but
#Text= together bend directly backwards, and they have no dewlaps.
#Text=We saw
#Text= several that were as big as a well-grown European ox, and there must be
#Text= some much larger; for Mr Banks saw a pair of horns which measured, from
#Text= tip to tip, three feet nine inches and a half, across their widest
#Text= diameter, four feet one inch and a half, and in the whole sweep of their
#Text= semicircle in front, seven feet six inches and a half.
#Text=It must, however,
#Text= be observed, that a buffalo here of any given size, does not weigh above
#Text= half as much as an ox of the same size in England: Those that we guessed
#Text= to weigh four hundred weight, did not weigh more than two hundred and
#Text=fifty; the reason is, that so late in the dry season the bones are very
#Text= thinly covered with flesh: There is not an ounce of fat in a whole
#Text= carcase, and the flanks are literally nothing but skin and bone: The
#Text= flesh, however, is well tasted and juicy, and I suppose better than the
#Text= flesh of an English ox would be if he was to starve in this sun-burnt
#Text= country.
#Text=The horses are from eleven to twelve hands high, but though they are
#Text= small, they are spirited and nimble, especially in pacing, which is
#Text= their common step: The inhabitants generally ride them without a saddle,
#Text= and with no better bridle than a halter.
#Text=The sheep are of the kind which
#Text= in England are called Bengal sheep, and differ from ours in many
#Text= particulars.
#Text=They are covered with hair instead of wool; their ears are
#Text= very large, and hang down under their horns, and their noses are arched;
#Text= they are thought to have a general resemblance to a goat, and for that
#Text= reason are frequently called _cabritos_: Their flesh we thought the
#Text= worst mutton we had ever eaten, being as lean as that of the buffaloes,
#Text= and without flavour.
#Text=The hogs, however, were some of the fattest we had
#Text= ever seen, though, as we were told, their principal food is the outside
#Text= husks of rice, and a palm syrup dissolved in water.[106] The fowls are
#Text=gather when young, and toast in the ear.
#Text=Here is also a great variety of
#Text= kidney-beans, and lentiles which they call _Cadjang_, and which make a
#Text= considerable part of the food of the common people; besides millet, yams
#Text= both wet and dry, sweet potatoes, and European potatoes, which are very
#Text= good, but not cultivated in great plenty.
#Text=In the gardens, there are
#Text= cabbages, lettuces, cucumbers, radishes, the white radishes of China,
#Text= which boil almost as well as a turnip; carrots, parsley, celery, pigeon
#Text= peas, the egg plant, which, broiled and eaten with pepper and salt, is
#Text= very delicious; a kind of greens resembling spinnage; onions, very
#Text= small, but excellent; and asparagus: Besides some European plants of a
#Text= strong smell, particularly sage, hysop, and rue.
#Text=Sugar is also produced
#Text= here in immense quantities; very great crops of the finest and largest
#Text= canes that can be imagined are produced with very little care, and yield
#Text= a much larger proportion of sugar than the canes in the West Indies.
#Text=White sugar is sold here at two-pence half-penny a pound; and the
#Text= molasses makes the arrack, of which, as of rum, it is the chief
#Text= ingredient; a small quantity of rice, and some cocoa-nut wine, being
#Text= added, chiefly, I suppose, to give it flavour.
#Text=A small quantity of
#Text= indigo is also produced here, not as an article of trade, but merely for
#Text= home consumption.[147]
#Text=from a hot-house in England: They are however so luxuriant in their
#Text= growth that most of them have two or three crowns, and a great number of
#Text= suckers from the bottom of the fruit; of these Mr Banks once counted
#Text= nine, and they are so forward that very often while they still adhered
#Text= to the parent plant they shot out their fruit, which, by the time the
#Text= large one became ripe, were of no inconsiderable size.
#Text=We several times
#Text= saw three upon one apple, and were told that a plant once produced a
#Text= cluster of nine, besides the principal: This indeed was considered as so
#Text= great a curiosity, that it was preserved in sugar, and sent to the
#Text= Prince of Orange.
#Text=
#Text= 2.
#Text=Sweet oranges.
#Text=These are very good, but while we were here, sold for
#Text= six-pence a piece.
#Text=
#Text= 3.
#Text=Pumplemoeses, which in the West Indies are called Shaddocks.
#Text=These
#Text= were well flavoured, but not juicy; their want of juice, however, was an
#Text= accidental effect of the season.
#Text=
#Text= 4.
#Text=Lemons.
#Text=These were very scarce; but the want of them was amply
#Text= compensated by the plenty of limes.
#Text=
#Text= 5.
#Text=Limes.
#Text=These were excellent, and to be bought at about twelve-pence a
#Text= hundred.
#Text=We saw only two or three Seville oranges, which were almost all
#Text= rind; and there are many sorts, both of oranges and lemons, which I
#Text= shall not particularly mention, because they are neither esteemed by
#Text= Europeans nor the natives themselves.
#Text=
#Text= 6.
#Text=Mangos.
#Text=This fruit during our stay was so infested with maggots,
#Text= which bred in the inside of them, that scarcely one in three was
#Text= eatable; and the best of them were much inferior to those of Brazil:
#Text= They are generally compared by Europeans to a melting peach, which
#Text= indeed they resemble in softness and sweetness, but certainly fall much
#Text= short in flavour.
#Text=The climate here, we were told, is too hot and damp
#Text= for them; but there are as many sorts of them as there are of apples in
#Text= England, and some are much superior to others.
#Text=One sort, which is called
#Text= _Mangha Cowani_, has so strong a smell that a European can scarcely bear
#Text= one in the room.
#Text=These, however, the natives are fond of.
#Text=The three
#Text= sorts which are generally preferred, are the _Mangha Doodool_, the
#Text= _Mangha Santock_, and the _Mangha Gure_.
#Text=
#Text=7.
#Text=Bananas.
#Text=Of these also there are innumerable sorts, but three only
#Text= are good; the _Pissang Mas_, the _Pissang Radja_, and the _Pissang
#Text= Ambou_: All these have a pleasant vinous taste, and the rest are useful
#Text= in different ways; some are fried in batter, and others are boiled and
#Text= eaten as bread.
#Text=There is one which deserves the particular notice of the
#Text= botanist, because, contrary to the nature of its tribe, it is full of
#Text= seeds, and is therefore called _Pissang Batu_, or _Pissang Bidjie_; it
#Text= his however no excellence to recommend it to the taste, but the Malays
#Text= use it as a remedy for the flux.
#Text=
#Text= 8.
#Text=Grapes.
#Text=These are not in great perfection, but they are very dear;
#Text= for we could not buy a moderate bunch for less than a shilling or
#Text= eighteen-pence.
#Text=
#Text= 9.
#Text=Tamarinds.
#Text=These are in great plenty, and very cheap: The people,
#Text= however, do not put them up in the manner practised by the West Indians,
#Text= but cure them with salt, by which means they become a black mass, so
#Text= disagreeable to the sight and taste, that few Europeans chuse to meddle
#Text= with them.
#Text=
#Text=10.
#Text=Water melons.
#Text=These are in great plenty, and very good.
#Text=
#Text= 11.
#Text=Pumpkins.
#Text=These are beyond comparison the most useful fruit that can
#Text= be carried to sea; for they will keep without any care several months,
#Text= and with sugar and lemon-juice, make a pye that can scarcely be
#Text= distinguished from one made of the best of apples; and with pepper and
#Text= salt, they are a substitute for turnips, not to be despised.
#Text=
#Text= 12 Papaws.
#Text=This fruit when it is ripe is full of seeds, and almost
#Text= without flavour; but if when it is green it is pared, and the core taken
#Text= out, it is better than the best turnip.
#Text=
#Text= 13.
#Text=Guava.
#Text=This fruit is much commended by the inhabitants of our
#Text= islands in the West Indies, who probably have a better sort than we met
#Text= with here, where the smell of them was so disagreeably strong that it
#Text= made some of us sick; those who tasted them said, that the flavour was
#Text= equally rank.
#Text=
#Text= 14.
#Text=Sweet sop.
#Text=The _Annona Squammosa_ of Linnæus.
#Text=This is also a
#Text= West-Indian fruit: It consists only of a mass of large kernels, from
#Text=which a small proportion of pulp may be sucked, which is very sweet, but
#Text= has little flavour.
#Text=
#Text= 15.
#Text=Custard apple.
#Text=The _Annona Reticulata_ of Linnæus.
#Text=The quality of
#Text= this fruit is well expressed by its English name, which it acquired in
#Text= the West Indies; for it is as like a custard, and a good one too, as can
#Text= be imagined.
#Text=
#Text= 16.
#Text=The cashew apple.
#Text=This is seldom eaten on account of its
#Text= astringency.
#Text=The nut that grows upon the top of it is well known in
#Text= Europe.
#Text=
#Text= 17.
#Text=The cocoa-nut.
#Text=This is also well known in Europe: There are several
#Text= sorts, but the best of those we found here is called _Calappi Edjou_,
#Text= and is easily known by the redness of the flesh between the skin and the
#Text= shell.
#Text=
#Text= 18.
#Text=Mangostan.
#Text=The _Garcinia Mangostana_ of Linnæus.
#Text=This fruit, which
#Text= is peculiar to the East Indies, is about the size of the crab apple, and
#Text= of a deep red-wine colour: On the top of it is the figure of five or six
#Text=small triangles joined in a circle, and at the bottom several hollow
#Text= green leaves, which are remains of the blossom.
#Text=When they are to be
#Text= eaten, the skin, or rather flesh, must be taken off, under which are
#Text= found six or seven white kernels, placed in a circular order, and the
#Text= pulp with which these are enveloped, is the fruit, than which nothing
#Text= can be more delicious: It is a happy mixture of the tart and the sweet,
#Text= which is no less wholesome than pleasant; and with the sweet orange,
#Text= this fruit is allowed in any quantity to those who are afflicted with
#Text= fevers, either of the putrid or inflammatory kind.
#Text=
#Text= 19.
#Text=The jamboo.
#Text=The _Eugenia Mallaccensis_ of Linnæus.
#Text=This fruit is of
#Text= a deep red colour, and an oval shape; the largest, which are always the
#Text= best, are not bigger than a small apple; they are pleasant and cooling,
#Text= though they have not much flavour.
#Text=
#Text= 20.
#Text=The jambu-eyer.
#Text=A species of the _Eugenia_ of Linnæus.
#Text=Of this fruit
#Text= there are two sorts of a similar shape, resembling a bell, but differing
#Text= in colour; one being red, the other white.
#Text=They somewhat exceed a large
#Text= cherry in size, and in taste have neither flavour nor even sweetness,
#Text= containing nothing but a watery juice, slightly acidulated; yet their
#Text=coolness recommends them in this hot country.
#Text=
#Text= 21.
#Text=Jambu-eyer mauwar.
#Text=The _Eugenia Jambos_ of Linnæus.
#Text=This is more
#Text= grateful to the smell than the taste: In taste it resembles the conserve
#Text= of roses, and in smell the fresh scent of those flowers.
#Text=
#Text= 22.
#Text=The pomegranate.
#Text=This is the same fruit that is known by the same
#Text= name all over Europe.
#Text=
#Text= 23.
#Text=Durion.
#Text=A fruit that in shape resembles a small melon, but the skin
#Text= is covered with sharp conical spines, whence its name; for _dure_, in
#Text= the Malay language, signifies prickle.
#Text=When it is ripe, it divides
#Text= longitudinally into seven or eight compartments, each of which contains
#Text= six or seven nuts, not quite so large as chesnuts, which are covered
#Text= with a substance that in colour and consistence very much resembles
#Text= thick cream: This is the part that is eaten, and the natives are fond of
#Text= it to excess.
#Text=To Europeans it is generally disagreeable at first; for in
#Text= taste it somewhat resembles a mixture of cream, sugar, and onions; and
#Text= in the smell, the onions predominate.
#Text=
#Text=24.
#Text=Nanca.
#Text=This fruit, which in some parts of India is called Jakes,
#Text= has, like the Durion, a smell very disagreeable to strangers, and
#Text= somewhat resembling that of mellow apples mixed with garlic: The flavour
#Text= is not more adapted to the general taste.
#Text=In some countries that are
#Text= favourable to it, it is said to grow to an immense size.
#Text=Rumphius
#Text= relates, that it is sometimes so large that a man cannot easily lift it;
#Text= and we were told by a Malay, that at Madura it is sometimes so large as
#Text= not to be carried but by the united efforts of two men.
#Text=At Batavia,
#Text= however, they never exceed the size of a large melon, which in shape
#Text= they very much resemble: They are covered with angular prickles, like
#Text= the shootings of some crystals, which however are not hard enough to
#Text= wound those who handle them.
#Text=
#Text= 25.
#Text=Champada.
#Text=This differs from the Nanca in little except size, it not
#Text= being so big. .
#Text=
#Text= 26.
#Text=Rambutan.
#Text=This is a fruit little known to Europeans.
#Text=In appearance
#Text= it very much resembles a chesnut with the husk on, and like that, is
#Text= covered with small points, which are soft, and of a deep red colour:
#Text= Under this skin is the fruit, and within the fruit a stone; the eatable
#Text=part thereof is small in quantity, but its acid is perhaps more
#Text= agreeable than any other in the whole vegetable kingdom.
#Text=
#Text= 27.
#Text=Jambolan.
#Text=This, in size and appearance, is not unlike a damascene;
#Text= but in taste is still more astringent, and therefore less agreeable.
#Text=
#Text= 28.
#Text=The Boa Bidarra, or _Rhamnus Jujuba_ of Linnæus.
#Text=This is a round
#Text= yellow fruit, about the size of a gooseberry; its flavour is like that
#Text= of an apple, but it has the astringency of a crab.
#Text=
#Text= 29.
#Text=Nam nam.
#Text=The _Cynometra Cauliflora_ of Linnæus.
#Text=This fruit in shape
#Text= somewhat resembles a kidney; it is about three inches long, and the
#Text= outside is very rough: It is seldom eaten raw, but fried with batter it
#Text= makes a good fritter.
#Text=
#Text=The Catappa, or _Terminalia Catappa_; and the Canare, the
#Text= _Canarium Commune_ of Linnæus, are both nuts, with kernels somewhat
#Text= resembling an almond; but the difficulty of breaking the shell is so
#Text= great, that they are no where publicly sold.
#Text=Those which we tasted were
#Text= gathered for curiosity by Mr Banks from the tree upon which they grew.
#Text=
#Text= 32.
#Text=The Madja, or _Limoni_ of Linnæus, contains, under a hard brittle
#Text= shell, a lightly acid pulp, which cannot be eaten without sugar; and
#Text= with it, is not generally thought pleasant.
#Text=
#Text= 33.
#Text=Suntul.
#Text=The _Trichilia_ of Linnæus.
#Text=This is the worst of all the
#Text= fruits that I shall particularly mention: In size and shape it resembles
#Text= the Madja, and within a thick skin contains kernels like those of the
#Text= Mangostan, the taste of which is both acid and astringent, and so
#Text= disagreeable, that we were surprised to see it exposed upon the
#Text= fruit-stalls.
#Text=
#Text=The Blimbing, or _Averrhoa Belimbi_; the Blimbing Besse, or
#Text= _Averrhoa Carambola_; and the Cherrema, or _Averrhoa Acida_ of Linnæus,
#Text= are three species of one genus; and though they differ in shape, are
#Text= nearly of the same taste.
#Text=The Blimbing Besse is the sweetest: the other
#Text= two are so austerely acid, that they cannot be used without dressing;
#Text= they make, however, excellent pickles and sour sauce.
#Text=
#Text= 37.
#Text=The Salack, or _Calamus Rotang Zalacca_ of Linnæus.
#Text=This is the
#Text=we were inclined to doubt it: They have indeed the _palearia_ or
#Text= _dewlap_, which naturalists make the distinguishing characteristic of
#Text= the European species, but they certainly are found wild, not only in
#Text= Java, but several of the eastern islands.
#Text=The flesh of those that we eat
#Text= at Batavia, had a finer grain than European beef, but it was less juicy,
#Text= and miserably lean.
#Text=Buffaloes are plenty, but the Dutch never eat them,
#Text= nor will they drink their milk, being prepossessed with a notion that
#Text= both are unwholesome, and tend to produce fevers; though the natives and
#Text= Chinese eat both, without any injury to their health.
#Text=The sheep are of
#Text= the kind which have long ears that hang down, and hair instead of wool:
#Text= The flesh of these is hard and tough, and in every respect the worst
#Text= mutton we ever saw.
#Text=We found here, however, a few Cape sheep, which are
#Text= excellent, but so dear that we gave five-and-forty shillings a-piece for
#Text= four of them, the heaviest of which weighed only five-and-forty pounds.
#Text=The goats are not better than the sheep; but the hogs, especially the
#Text= Chinese breed, are incomparable, and so fat, that the purchaser agrees
#Text= for the lean separately.
#Text=The butcher, who is always a Chinese, without
#Text= the least scruple cuts off as much of the fat as he is desired, and
#Text= afterwards sells it to his countrymen, who melt it down, and eat it
#Text= instead of butter with their rice: But notwithstanding the excellence of
#Text=other places, that vanity gets the better even of appetite: The cheap
#Text= fish, most of which is of the best kind, is the food only of slaves, and
#Text= that which is dear, only because it is scarce, and very much inferior in
#Text= every respect, is placed upon the tables of the rich.
#Text=A. sensible
#Text= house-keeper once spoke to us freely upon the subject.
#Text="I know," said
#Text= he, "as well as you, that I could purchase a better dish of fish for a
#Text= shilling, than what now costs me ten; but if I should make so good a use
#Text= of my money, I should here be as much despised, as you would be in
#Text= Europe, if you were to cover your table with offals, fit only for
#Text= beggars, or dogs."
#Text=Turtle is also found here, but it is neither so sweet nor so fat as the
#Text= West-Indian turtle, even in London; such as it is, however, we should
#Text= consider it as a dainty; but the Dutch, among other singularities, do
#Text= not eat it.
#Text=We saw some lizards, or Iguanas, here of a very large size;
#Text= we were told that some were as thick as a man  '  s thigh, and Mr Banks shot
#Text= one that was five feet long: The flesh of this animal proved to be very
#Text= good food.

#Text= twelve: In this state it has an agreeable sweetness, and will not

#Text=In the other two states it has undergone a fermentation, and

#Text=A liquor called Tuac is also made from the
#Text= cocoa-nut tree, but this is used chiefly to put into the arrack, for in
#Text= that which is good it is an essential ingredient.

#Text= people, that in prowling the earth "the devil walketh through dry

#Text=Mr Banks once asked, whether they thought Satan spent the
#Text= money, or eat the victuals?
#Text=he was answered, that as to the money, it
#Text= was considered rather as a mulct upon an offender, than a gift to him
#Text= who had enjoined it, and that therefore, if it was devoted by the
#Text= dreamer, it mattered not into whose hands it came, and they supposed
#Text= that it was generally the prize of some stranger who wandered that way;
#Text= but as to the meat, they were clearly of opinion that although the devil
#Text= did not eat the gross parts, yet, by bringing his mouth near it, he
#Text= sucked out all its savour without changing its position, so that
#Text= afterwards it was as tasteless as water.[152]
